summary.text: A lens is a transparent device, usually of glass or plastic, that focuses or spreads a beam of light by refraction.
Unlike a prism, a lens can focus light into an image, which is why telescopes, binoculars, cameras and glasses all rely on lenses.
Most lenses have two spherical surfaces, each convex, concave or flat, and a single lens cannot bring all colours to one focus, which led to compound lenses.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: From the Latin word for a lentil, which a double-convex lens resembles

facts.label: Achromatic lens
facts.value: Invented by Chester Moore Hall in England in 1733

facts.label: Fresnel lens
facts.value: First fully used in a lighthouse in 1823

facts.label: Lens axis
facts.value: The line joining the centres of the spheres forming the surfaces

facts.label: Telescope
facts.value: The refracting telescope appeared in 1608 in the Netherlands

items.prompt: A beam of sunlight goes through a glass prism and a glass lens. In what way does the lens act differently?

options.label: It bends light but never forms an image
It reflects light instead of refracting it
It focuses light to form an image, while a prism only redirects it
It slows light while the prism leaves speed unchanged

items.explain: A lens can focus light to form an image, whereas a prism refracts light without focusing it.

items.prompt: A lighthouse needs light visible from very far away. Why did builders turn to Fresnel lenses rather than one huge ordinary convex lens?

options.label: They use less material because the lens is cut into concentric rings
They are made of a clearer glass than ordinary lenses
They produce their own light and need no lamp
They are flat mirrors that need no glass at all

items.explain: A conventional convex lens big enough would cost too much, so Fresnel lenses use less material through concentric annular sectioning.

items.prompt: In the 1700s opticians kept reshaping lens surfaces to cure colour fringes, assuming the surfaces were badly curved. What did the theory of refraction show?

options.label: Better polishing would remove the fringes in time
The fringes came from impurities inside the glass
A perfectly spherical surface fixes the problem completely
No single-element lens could bring all colours to one focus

items.explain: The errors were not due to flawed surface shapes; no single lens can focus all colours together, which led to compound achromatic lenses.

items.prompt: A person's eye sees blurred lines in one direction but not another. Which kind of lens corrects that?

options.label: A lens with equal curvature in every direction
A toric lens with different focal power in different directions
A thick flat plate of glass with no curve
A prism that bends light without focusing it

items.explain: Toric (sphero-cylindrical) lenses have two different radii of curvature in perpendicular planes, giving different power in different meridians, which corrects astigmatism.

items.prompt: In the 12th century, readers used a 'reading stone' to enlarge text. What was it?

options.label: A small mirror laid flat on the page
A glass sphere cut in half and set on the page
A thin sheet of polished rock with a hole
A prism held over the lines of writing

items.explain: Reading stones were primitive plano-convex lenses, made by cutting a glass sphere in half.

items.prompt: The compound microscope and the refracting telescope both first appeared in spectacle-making towns. Why there?

options.label: Those towns had the only lenses made of crystal
Astronomers there had already worked out the theory
Law required every town to build instruments for ships
Practical work with lenses by spectacle makers led to them

items.explain: The practical development and experimentation with lenses in the spectacle-making centres led to these inventions.

paragraphs.heading: What a lens is
paragraphs.text: A lens is a device that lets light through and uses refraction to bring a beam together or spread it apart. A simple lens is one piece of transparent material, while a compound lens is built from several simple lenses, called elements, usually lined up along a shared axis. Lenses are made from materials like glass or plastic and are ground, polished or moulded into shape. Unlike a prism, which bends light without focusing it, a lens can focus light into an image.

paragraphs.heading: Where lenses are used
paragraphs.text: Lenses are used in imaging devices such as telescopes, binoculars and cameras. Glasses use them to correct faults of vision such as myopia and hypermetropia. The name comes from lēns, the Latin word for a lentil, because a lens that bulges on both sides has a lentil's shape. Devices that focus or spread other kinds of waves are called lenses too, including microwave, electron, acoustic and even explosive lenses.

paragraphs.heading: Lenses in the ancient world
paragraphs.text: How far back real lenses go is debated. Some scholars read the archaeological evidence as showing wide use of lenses across several thousand years of antiquity, while others think most ancient examples were decorative, apart from some burning glasses. The Nimrud lens, a piece of rock crystal from the 7th century BCE, may or may not have served as a magnifying glass or a burning glass. The oldest certain mention of a lens used as a burning glass comes in Aristophanes's play The Clouds, from 424 BCE, and Pliny the Elder confirms that the Romans knew of burning glasses.

paragraphs.heading: From reading stones to telescopes
paragraphs.text: Between the 11th and 13th centuries people used reading stones, simple lenses first made by cutting a glass sphere in half. Spectacles were invented in Northern Italy during the later 1200s as an improvement on them. That began an industry of grinding and polishing spectacle lenses, first in Venice and Florence and later in the Netherlands and Germany. Hands-on experiment with lenses in the Dutch spectacle-making centres led to the compound microscope around 1595 and the refracting telescope in 1608.

paragraphs.heading: The colour problem
paragraphs.text: Once telescopes and microscopes existed, people in the 17th and early 18th centuries tried many lens shapes to fix the colour errors they saw. Opticians varied the curvature, wrongly assuming the errors came from defects in the spherical form of the surfaces. Theory and experiment showed instead that no lens made of a single element could bring every colour to one focus. The answer was the compound achromatic lens, invented by Chester Moore Hall in England in 1733 and also claimed by John Dollond in a 1758 patent.

paragraphs.heading: Lens shapes
paragraphs.text: Most lenses are spherical, meaning each of their two surfaces is part of the surface of a sphere. Each surface can be convex, bulging outward, concave, dipping inward, or flat. The line joining the centres of those spheres is the lens axis. Toric lenses instead have two different curvatures in two directions at right angles, so they focus with a different strength along different lines. Eyeglass lenses of this kind are used to correct astigmatism.

paragraphs.heading: The lighthouse lens
paragraphs.text: Growing trade across the Atlantic drove the building of modern lighthouses in the 18th century. To be seen from as far away as possible, an ordinary convex lens would have had to be very large, which made cost, design and building harder. The Fresnel lens met this problem by using less material, divided into concentric rings. It was first fully installed in a lighthouse in 1823.
